title: Inheritance in practice
hook: fixed shares for family, and up to a third by will

segments.voice: Yesterday, children's rights, and your line: fair to each. A father walked his son to the Prophet, and the gift went back.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas lies sick in Mecca, sure he is about to die. He has some wealth and one daughter to inherit from him. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ comes to visit, and Sa'd asks straight out: may I give all my wealth away in charity? It sounds like a beautiful question. The Prophet says no. Then half? No. Then a third? A third, the Prophet answers, and a third is a lot. Tradition says Sa'd recovered. But that bedside bargain became a line in Islamic law.
screen: `SA'D ON HIS SICKBED.` → `ALL? NO. HALF? NO.` → `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.`

segments.voice: Islamic inheritance works in two layers. The first is fixed by the Qur'an. In surah four, God names the shares: what children receive, what parents receive, what a husband or wife receives. The verses call them an ordinance from God, and the jurists built a whole science around them, called fara'id, the obligatory shares. You don't choose these. The second layer is yours. Before the shares are divided, the debts are paid and the will is carried out, and the will can reach up to a third of what is left. That third is where a person can remember a friend, a cause, a mosque, a stranger who was kind. One limit: a report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says there is no bequest to an heir. Those who already have a share from the Qur'an can't be given extra by will; the third is for people the shares don't reach. And the Prophet gave Sa'd a reason. In Sahih al-Bukhari, he says leaving your heirs well off is better than leaving them dependent, holding out their hands to people. So the limit isn't a limit on generosity. It points generosity two ways at once: to family, through the shares, and to the wider world, through the third. A family may sit with a scholar to work out the exact shares, and the schools disagree on some rarer cases. But the shape holds: the debts, the third, then the shares.
screen: `LAYER ONE: SHARES FIXED IN SURAH FOUR.` · `LAYER TWO: A WILL, UP TO A THIRD.` · `NO BEQUEST TO AN HEIR.` · `LEAVE THEM WELL OFF, NOT DEPENDENT.`

segments.voice: Write a very simple will, only in your head for now: start with what you owe, anyone you'd want paid back, any promise you'd want kept. Then think about your third, not the money but the people outside your family: a teacher, a neighbor, a place that fed you once. Hold one name, and if it feels right, you can write it down later.
Inheritance in practice. Fixed shares for the family from the Qur'an, and up to a third by will for those the shares don't reach. Today's word.
Your line: a third by will. Family through the shares, the wider world through the third. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: When a Muslim dies, debts are paid first, then any will of up to a third is carried out, and the rest is divided among family members by the shares set out in surah four, often with a scholar's help.

chat.says: Can a Muslim leave everything to charity in their will?
options: Up to a third. The rest goes to family in the shares the Qur'an fixes.
All of it, even if the heirs object. A will can override the shares.
No. Wills aren't allowed; the Qur'an's shares decide every last coin.
chat.meaning: The Prophet told Sa'd: a third, and a third is a lot. The family's shares are fixed by the Qur'an.

notes: Sa'd's report: confirm details (in Mecca, during the farewell pilgrimage in some versions; one daughter; all/half/third; 'a third, and a third is a lot'; heirs rich rather than dependent). 'Recovered and lived on' is in some versions of the report; confirm.
Qur'an 4:11–12 paraphrased; 'an ordinance from God' paraphrases the verse's own language; confirm.
Order debts, then will, then shares: from 4:11–12 ('after any bequest... or debt') and jurists' ordering of debts first; confirm.
'No bequest to an heir' unless other heirs consent (some schools); not mentioned in voice; Keeper may want it.
